title: Maximum subarray sum: brute force vs running sums vs Kadane's scan
problem_statement: Given a list a[0..n-1] of n >= 1 integers (negative values allowed), compute the maximum of a[i] + a[i+1] + ... + a[j] over all 0 <= i <= j < n, i.e. the largest sum of a non-empty contiguous subarray.

input.size_measure: n integers of bounded size (the harness draws them from [-100, 100]); arithmetic on them is O(1).

algorithms.name: brute force (sum every subarray)
algorithms.idea: For every pair i <= j, add up a[i..j] from scratch and keep the largest sum.
algorithms.pseudocode: best = a[0]; for i in 0..n-1: for j in i..n-1: s = a[i] + ... + a[j] (a loop); best = max(best, s)
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n^3) on every input: the innermost loop runs n(n+1)(n+2)/6 times
algorithms.correctness: Exhaustive over all n(n+1)/2 non-empty contiguous subarrays.

algorithms.name: running sums
algorithms.idea: For each start i, extend the subarray one element at a time; the sum of a[i..j] is the sum of a[i..j-1] plus a[j].
algorithms.pseudocode: best = a[0]; for i in 0..n-1: s = 0; for j in i..n-1: s = s + a[j]; best = max(best, s)
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n^2) on every input: n(n+1)/2 inner steps
algorithms.correctness: Still exhaustive over all subarrays; only the way each sum is obtained changes.

algorithms.name: Kadane's algorithm (linear scan)
algorithms.idea: Scan left to right keeping the best sum of a subarray ending at the current position: it is either the current element alone or the previous best extended by it.
algorithms.pseudocode: best = cur = a[0]; for j in 1..n-1: cur = a[j] if cur < 0 else cur + a[j]; best = max(best, cur)
algorithms.correctness: Invariant after reading a[0..j]: cur is the best sum of a non-empty subarray ending at j, and best is the best sum of any non-empty subarray of a[0..j]. A subarray ending at j is a[j] alone or extends one ending at j - 1, and the best extension uses the best such one (Bentley 1984; CLRS Exercise 4.1-5).

relationship: Three polynomial algorithms in a chain: reusing the previous sum turns Theta(n^3) into Theta(n^2), and keeping only the best subarray ending at each position turns Theta(n^2) into Theta(n). Each step is a strict asymptotic improvement for the same problem.

sources.title: Programming pearls: algorithm design techniques
sources.note: Presents the cubic, quadratic, divide-and-conquer Theta(n log n) and linear (credited to J. Kadane) algorithms for this problem.

sources.authors: Cormen, T. H.; Leiserson, C. E.; Rivest, R. L.; Stein, C.
sources.title: Introduction to Algorithms (3rd ed.)
sources.note: Section 4.1 (the maximum-subarray problem, divide and conquer) and Exercise 4.1-5 (the linear-time scan).

verification.method: V1: all three implementations agree with each other and with an independent oracle, the CLRS 4.1 divide-and-conquer algorithm (in harness.py), on random lists from [-100, 100] (some all-negative, some all-non-negative), n = 1..10, 15, 20, 40, 60, 200 and 1000 (brute force up to n = 60, running sums up to n = 200). V2: runtimes fit n^3 (n = 50..400), n^2 (n = 100..3200) and n (n = 3000..1000000). All three do the same amount of work on every input of a given length, so random inputs are worst-case inputs.

caveats: The problem requires a non-empty subarray; the variant that allows the empty subarray (answer max(0, ...)) differs only on all-negative inputs. Kadane's scan is optimal up to a constant factor, since a correct algorithm must read every element: changing an unread element to a large value changes the answer.
notes: The divide-and-conquer Theta(n log n) algorithm (CLRS 4.1, also in Bentley's column) sits between the quadratic and linear algorithms; it is used here as the independent V1 oracle rather than as a fourth recorded algorithm. Bentley attributes the problem to U. Grenander's work on pattern matching in digitized images.
